amendments.rule: **A purpose `לְ` + infinitive construct recast as a finite clause gives the complementizer to the preposition and the supplied subject and modal to the infinitive.** The ASV writes *that men may bring*, *that I may be glorified*. This is rule 48's division outside the privative `מִן`, and for the same reason: the complementizer is what the preposition contributes, while a supplied subject pronoun and a separately written modal belong to the verb, as rule 17 keeps a subject pronoun with its verb. The corpus puts the *that* on the preposition in 28 units across 17 chapters and never on the infinitive, so this too is settled. Where the ASV writes no English word at all for the preposition there is nothing to place, and the `לְ` goes `unrepresented` under rule 40. **Read that as no word, not as no complementizer.** The complementizer is what a finite recasting spends on the preposition, but a recasting that makes the infinitive an English gerund or a bare verbal noun writes an ordinary preposition in that same position, and that word is the `לְ`'s on the same terms: `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ` → *by keeping his covenant*, `לִשְׁלֹחַ מַלְאָכָיו` → *in sending his ambassadors*, `לְהָפֵר בְּרִית` → *by breaking the covenant*, `לָצֶקֶת` → *for casting*, `לֶאֱכֹל` → *an end of eating*. The corpus aligns a `לְ` before an infinitive construct to a written *to* in 583 units, to *that* in 81, and to *for*, *in*, *of*, *by*, *after* or *when* in 53 more, against 527 marked `unrepresented`; the two groups do not disagree, because every unrepresented one is a recasting that writes no function word at all — *left off building*, *the building of the house*. So ask whether a word is written before reaching for rule 40, and do not read the gerund itself as the recasting that silences the preposition. **Where two such `לְ` + infinitive phrases stand in one clause and the ASV writes one complementizer and one preposition, count them as this rule's last sentence directs rather than taking them in linear order.** `לִשְׁמֹר אֶת־בְּרִיתוֹ לְעָמְדָהּ` → *that by keeping his covenant it might stand* gives *by* to the `לְ` of the gerund and *that* to the `לְ` whose infinitive the finite clause renders: the ASV fronts the complementizer ahead of the gerund adjunct, and that reordering says nothing about which preposition it answers to. **A temporal preposition before an infinitive construct is read the same way.** Where `בְּ` or `כְּ` + infinitive is recast as a finite temporal clause — `בְּחֻמָּם` → *When they are heated*, `בְּלֶכְתּוֹ` → *when he went*, `כְּבֹאֲךָ` → *When thou comest*, `כְּכַלֹּתְךָ` → *when thou hast made an end* — the preposition takes the *when*, the infinitive keeps the verb, and the suffix takes the subject pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18. The corpus aligns `בְּ` to *when* in 45 units, so the temporal case is settled on the same footing as the purpose case. Read the preposition that is present rather than its lemma: a `לְ` heading such a phrase goes the same way even where its object is the noun rather than the infinitive, as in `לְקוֹל תִּתּוֹ` → *When he uttereth his voice*. **But only a preposition that still has an English word to take can take it.** Where no preposition is present and the construct relation itself is what the English *when* realizes, rule 19 puts that word on the *nomen rectum*, which is the infinitive: `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` → *at the time when it is trodden* gives *at the time* to `עֵת` and *when ... is trodden* to the infinitive. **And a preposition on which the ASV has already spent its own English word is in the same position as an absent one.** Where the preposition heads a construct noun, the ASV writes a word for that preposition and a second temporal word besides, the second answers to the construct relation and not to the preposition, so rule 19 puts it on the *nomen rectum*: `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` → *in the day when they shall make it* gives *in* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, leaving *when they shall make* to the infinitive, whose own suffix takes the pronoun rule 18 gives it. Count the ASV's function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s and rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s: a preposition holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, and giving it both would leave the construct's relation unrendered against rule 2. **But that count places the second word on a morpheme that is there to take it, and a noun the projection writes as an absolute has no rectum standing under it.** Where the preposition heads a noun MACULA tags absolute — as it does where a finite clause rather than an infinitive construct or another nominal follows the noun — no construct relation is written in the phrase at all, so rule 19 has nothing to place the second temporal word on: that word answers to no morpheme in the clause and is its own `added` unit under rule 55, while the preposition and the noun each keep the English written for them. `בְּיוֹם קָרָאתִי` → *In* ***the day*** ***that*** *I called* gives *In* to the `בְּ` and *the day* to `יוֹם`, the determiner supplied under rule 15, leaves *I called* to the finite verb, and marks the *that* `added`. Read MACULA's morphology rather than the pointing, exactly as rule 29 directs, and read what stands under the noun: an infinitive construct or another nominal under a construct noun is a rectum and the preceding sentences govern, and a finite clause under an absolute noun is not one. Rule 46 does not reach such a word either, since the noun the ASV writes before the clause is a written antecedent and that rule's headless case governs a clause with none. And where an apodosis follows whose waw the ASV leaves unrendered, that waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 and is not a home for the supplied word, which stands ahead of the temporal clause rather than at the apodosis's head, exactly as rule 45 reads a *that* written inside its frame. **Where no preposition stands before the infinitive construct at all, the English infinitive marker *to* belongs to the infinitive's own unit and is never `added`.** English writes no bare infinitive complement, so that word is what the infinitive itself licenses, exactly as rule 15 gives a supplied *a* to the noun that licenses it and rule 46 gives a supplied *them that* to a bare participle: `מֵאֵן בִּלְעָם הֲלֹךְ עִמָּנוּ` → *Balaam refuseth* ***to come*** *with us* and `הֲיָכוֹל אוּכַל דַּבֵּר מְאוּמָה` → *have I now any power at all* ***to speak*** *anything* each give the *to* to the infinitive, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24. Read whether a preposition is present before reaching for this sentence, since one and the same infinitive is read both ways in one chapter: `לַהֲלֹךְ עִמָּכֶם` → *to go with you* gives the written *to* to the `לְ` and only *go* to `הֲלֹךְ`, while the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds both words. And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before. **And the verb that takes such a bare *to* need not be an infinitive in the Hebrew.** Where a second Hebrew verb of any form — an imperative, a perfect, an imperfect — stands with no preposition on it and the ASV subordinates it to a governing verb as an English infinitive complement, the written *to* is what that English infinitive licenses and it joins the subordinated verb's own unit, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24, exactly as the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds it: `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste* ***to answer*** *me* gives *to answer* to `עָנָה` and *Make haste* to `מַהֵר`, and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee* ***to hide*** *me* gives *to hide me* to `כָּסָה`. Read what the ASV made of the verb rather than what MACULA tags it, exactly as rule 19 reads a participle or infinitive the ASV has written as an English verb and rule 33 defers only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as one. Do not give such a *to* to the governing verb: a verb already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and rule 44's supplied-preposition clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, which a complementizing *to* standing before a second verb is not. Two limits. Where a preposition morpheme does stand before that verb it takes the word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And where the governing verb and the subordinated verb are one and the same morpheme — a causative or other verb the ASV renders by a light verb and a second verb, as `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me* ***to hear*** and `הוֹשִׁיבַנִי` → *hath made me* ***to dwell*** — rule 44 keeps the whole phrase in that morpheme's one unit, headed on the lexical complement, and there is nothing to allocate.
amendments.why: Rule 52's `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` sentence tells a pass to hand the second temporal word to the *nomen rectum*, and PSA.138.3 writes an English phrase indistinguishable from it — *In the day that I called* — with no rectum in the source: MACULA tags `יוֹם` Ncmsa and what follows is a finite verb, not an infinitive construct. A pass reading only that sentence would give the *that* to `קָרָאתִי` as a rectum, or fold it into `יוֹם`'s own unit against rule 51's principle, where the contract's own logic makes it `added` — rule 19 needs two written nominals, rule 46's headless case is barred by the written antecedent `יוֹם`, and rule 55 marks a subordinator no morpheme in the clause reaches. The amendment is narrow by construction: it reaches only a noun the projection tags absolute, so every construct-tagged case, including the whole `בְּ` → *when* corpus mass of 45 units and the `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` and `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` divisions, is left exactly as rule 52 already reads it, and it cannot contradict any precedent shown in this chapter's briefing. It also carries the paired count for the apodosis waw, which is where BSB disagreed with this chapter, so the two sides of the count are stated together rather than left to be rediscovered.

conventions: The italicized 'endureth' of חַסְדְּךָ לְעוֹלָם → *Thy lovingkindness ... endureth for ever* is read as the construction-supplied copula on the prepositional predicate: it joins the לְ unit, headed on *for* (rules 20 and 49), and is not a supplied lexical verb marked `added` under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause. Rule 20's subtraction decides it — dropping the word leaves the subject and its prepositional predicate standing, so what has gone is the link English writes and not the predication — and 'endureth' links without introducing any participant the Hebrew does not write, as *remain* does in that rule's list. The ASV italic corroborates the supply and decides nothing (rule 7).

בְּיוֹם קָרָאתִי → *In the day that I called*: MACULA writes יוֹם absolute and a finite verb follows it, so no construct relation stands and rule 52's בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ division does not reach the phrase. בְּ takes *In*, יוֹם takes *the day* with the determiner rule 15 supplies, the finite verb takes *I called*, and the supplied *that* is its own `added` unit under rule 55, יוֹם being a written antecedent that puts rule 46 out of reach. The apodosis waw of וַתַּעֲנֵנִי, for which the ASV writes no connective, is `unrepresented` under rule 14; it is not a home for the *that*, which stands ahead of the temporal clause rather than at the apodosis's head. This is the chapter's only BSB disagreement.

And this reaches only a *to* the ASV has written: a modal's bare complement — *cannot go beyond* — has none to place, and a preposition the recasting leaves unrendered is `unrepresented` under rule 40 as before. **And the verb that takes such a bare *to* need not be an infinitive in the Hebrew.** Where a second Hebrew verb of any form — an imperative, a perfect, an imperfect — stands with no preposition on it and the ASV subordinates it to a governing verb as an English infinitive complement, the written *to* is what that English infinitive licenses and it joins the subordinated verb's own unit, headed on the lexical verb under rule 24, exactly as the bare `הֲלֹךְ` above holds it: `מַהֵר עֲנֵנִי` → *Make haste* ***to answer*** *me* gives *to answer* to `עָנָה` and *Make haste* to `מַהֵר`, and `אֵלֶיךָ כִסִּתִי` → *I flee unto thee* ***to hide*** *me* gives *to hide me* to `כָּסָה`. Read what the ASV made of the verb rather than what MACULA tags it, exactly as rule 19 reads a participle or infinitive the ASV has written as an English verb and rule 33 defers only to a governing verb the ASV has itself rendered as one. Do not give such a *to* to the governing verb: a verb already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and rule 44's supplied-preposition clause places a preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its own object, which a complementizing *to* standing before a second verb is not. Two limits. Where a preposition morpheme does stand before that verb it takes the word first, on the terms above, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And where the governing verb and the subordinated verb are one and the same morpheme — a causative or other verb the ASV renders by a light verb and a second verb, as `הַשְׁמִיעֵנִי` → *Cause me* ***to hear*** and `הוֹשִׁיבַנִי` → *hath made me* ***to dwell*** — rule 44 keeps the whole phrase in that morpheme's one unit, headed on the lexical complement, and there is nothing to allocate.
amended.why: Rule 52's `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` sentence tells a pass to hand the second temporal word to the *nomen rectum*, and PSA.138.3 writes an English phrase indistinguishable from it — *In the day that I called* — with no rectum in the source: MACULA tags `יוֹם` Ncmsa and what follows is a finite verb, not an infinitive construct. A pass reading only that sentence would give the *that* to `קָרָאתִי` as a rectum, or fold it into `יוֹם`'s own unit against rule 51's principle, where the contract's own logic makes it `added` — rule 19 needs two written nominals, rule 46's headless case is barred by the written antecedent `יוֹם`, and rule 55 marks a subordinator no morpheme in the clause reaches. The amendment is narrow by construction: it reaches only a noun the projection tags absolute, so every construct-tagged case, including the whole `בְּ` → *when* corpus mass of 45 units and the `עֵת הִדְרִיכָהּ` and `בְּיוֹם הֵעָשׂוֹתוֹ` divisions, is left exactly as rule 52 already reads it, and it cannot contradict any precedent shown in this chapter's briefing. It also carries the paired count for the apodosis waw, which is where BSB disagreed with this chapter, so the two sides of the count are stated together rather than left to be rediscovered.
